unitDescription.value:
In this unit, students investigate the characteristics and functional properties of sheet metal within the Materials and Technologies specialisations context. They explore the environmental impacts of metal production, specifically examining the galvanising process and the role of recycling in achieving sustainable designed solutions. Students develop essential graphical representation skills through a technical drawing booklet, mastering isometric and orthogonal techniques to communicate design ideas with precision, scale, and appropriate technical terminology.

Working in a workshop environment, students identify and apply safe working procedures to manage the production of a sheet metal dustpan. They demonstrate technical competence in marking out, cutting, folding, and joining materials using a range of specialised tools and equipment. Throughout the 10-week cycle, students develop project management skills and evaluate their manufacturing processes and final products against design criteria, considering the efficiency and durability of their solutions for a preferred future.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

title.value: Sheet Metal Dustpan Design and Production Project

description.value: Students document the investigation, design, and manufacture of a functional sheet metal dustpan within a technical folio and physical prototype. They apply graphical representation techniques to communicate design ideas and demonstrate technical competence in marking out, cutting, folding, and joining galvanised steel using specialised workshop equipment. The project requires students to justify material selections based on sustainability factors and evaluate the final solution against established design criteria.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8 students explain how people design, innovate and produce products, services and environments for preferred futures. For each of the 4 prescribed technologies contexts they explain how the features of technologies impact on design decisions, and create designed solutions based on analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create and adapt design ideas, processes and solutions, and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas and solutions to audiences using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools. They independently and collaboratively document and manage production processes to safely produce designed solutions.

activities.title: Galvanising Process and Metallurgy
activities.teacherDoes: Present a 0.6mm galvanised sheet sample. Point out the visible crystalline 'spangle' pattern. Explicitly explain the hot-dip galvanising process: immersing steel in molten zinc at ~450°C. Explain the metallurgical concept of 'sacrificial anode'—zinc corrodes preferentially to steel, providing galvanic protection even if the surface is scratched during fabrication. Model the completion of the 3-term definition table.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the sample steel pieces, observe the spangle coating, and complete the technical definition table for galvanising, sacrificial protection, and ductility.
activities.visibleInstructions: Define the 3 metallurgical terms in your table using complete sentences based on the teacher demonstration and board definitions.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does zinc protect steel from rusting even when the surface coating is scratched through to bare steel?
Expected: Zinc is electrochemically more reactive than iron, so it acts as a sacrificial anode and oxidises preferentially.
question: What mechanical property allows 0.6mm steel sheet to bend at 90 degrees in a panbrake without snapping?
Expected: Ductility (and malleability), allowing plastic deformation under shear and bending forces.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Hot-dip Galvanising: The industrial process of coating cleaned steel or iron in molten zinc at approximately 450°C to form a protective metallurgical barrier.
- Sacrificial Protection: Electrochemical protection where a more reactive metal (zinc) corrodes in preference to the underlying structural metal (steel).
- Ductility: The mechanical property of a material allowing it to undergo significant plastic deformation under tensile stress without fracturing.
activities.eLearning: Display high-resolution micrograph of zinc-iron metallurgical alloy layers on the central projector.
activities.transition: Keep your steel samples on the bench and turn to the Design Folio setup section in your workbook.

Sacrificial Protection: An electrochemical method where zinc oxidises preferentially to protect the exposed underlying steel from rusting.
Ductility: The ability of sheet metal to deform plastically and bend under force without cracking or structural failure.

activities.title: Sustainability and Lifecycle Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Lead a comparative discussion on environmental lifecycle analysis: compare raw untreated mild steel against hot-dip galvanised steel. Explain embodied energy: zinc refining requires high energy input initially, but galvanised products last 20–50 years without repainting, preventing premature landfill disposal. Emphasise that steel and zinc are 100% infinitely recyclable without quality degradation. Model categorising properties into the overlap comparison using the board. For example, '100% infinitely recyclable' applies to both materials, while 'sacrificial zinc layer' is exclusive to galvanised steel.

activities.questioning:
q: How does the extended lifespan of galvanised steel offset the high initial energy required to refine zinc?
Expected: Because it resists corrosion for decades without toxic maintenance paints, fewer replacement products need to be manufactured, reducing overall resource extraction over time.
q: Why is steel considered a cornerstone material of the circular economy?
Expected: It is 100% recyclable repeatedly through electric arc furnaces without loss of tensile strength or structural integrity.

activities.title: AS 1100 Line Conventions Modelling
activities.teacherDoes: Model standard AS 1100 line conventions on the drafting visualizer/whiteboard: continuous thick (0.5mm) for visible outlines/object lines, dashed medium (0.35mm) for hidden features or fold lines, thin chain (0.25mm long-dash/short-dot) for centre lines, and thin solid lines with arrowheads for dimension lines. Emphasise that in sheet metal drafting, a fold line that is bent away from the viewer is represented using hidden line conventions. Walk through the 4 numbered callouts on the dustpan drawing.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled drafting conventions, then annotate the 4 callouts on the dustpan engineering drawing with the correct line type name and its specific manufacturing purpose.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the dustpan drawing in your workbook, label callouts 1 to 4 with the correct AS 1100 line type and explain what each tells the sheet metal fabricator.
activities.questioning:
q: What would happen during sheet metal fabrication if a drafter drew a fold line as a thick solid object line instead of a dashed fold/hidden line?
Expected: The fabricator would cut along the line with the guillotine or snips instead of bending it in the panbrake, destroying the blank.
q: Why must dimension lines terminate in sharp, closed arrowheads?
Expected: To define the exact boundary points between which the measurement applies without ambiguity.
activities.scaffolding:
AS 1100 Standard Reference:
- Callout 1: Visible Outline (Continuous Thick 0.5mm) = Cut perimeter of the sheet
- Callout 2: Fold / Hidden Line (Dashed Medium 0.35mm) = 90-degree panbrake bend location
- Callout 3: Centre Line (Long dash, short dot Thin 0.25mm) = Axis of symmetry and hole centres
- Callout 4: Dimension Line (Thin solid with arrowheads) = Measured distance in millimetres

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how to calculate and draft dimensions at 1:2 scale using a steel rule. Model on the whiteboard: 'A full-size dustpan width is 220mm. At 1:2 scale, we divide the true dimension by 2 (220 / 2 = 110mm). We draw a 110mm line, but we label the dimension text as 220, because engineering drawings always state true physical size!' Guide students through 5 specific dustpan component calculations.

activities.questioning:
q: If a part is drawn at 1:2 scale, what measurement value is written on the dimension line—the drawn length or the true object size?
Expected: The true object size (full scale), because the fabricator works from the written number, not by measuring the paper.
q: Why is 1:2 scale preferred over 1:1 scale for drafting the dustpan on A4 drawing paper?
Expected: A full 250mm x 250mm blank cannot fit within the printable margins and title block of standard A4 paper.
activities.scaffolding:
Formula: Drawing Dimension (mm) = True Dimension (mm) / Scale Factor (2).
Examples:
- True 200mm -> 200 / 2 = 100mm on paper
- True 50mm -> 50 / 2 = 25mm on paper
- True 16mm hem -> 16 / 2 = 8mm on paper

lessons.title: Principles of Metal Deformation and Rigidity
lessons.learningGoal: Define the physical principles of metal deformation, spring-back, and the structural advantages of hems in sheet metal fabrication.

orientate.smartStart: On your mini-whiteboard, classify each of these three everyday items into 'elastic' (returns to shape) or 'plastic' (permanently deformed) when bent: a rubber band, a plastic ruler flexed slightly, and a bent steel paperclip.

activities.title: Metal Deformation Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Model the behaviour of 0.6mm galvanised sheet metal offcuts at the front demonstration bench. First, flex an offcut slightly and release it to demonstrate elastic deformation. Second, fold an offcut firmly past its yield point to demonstrate plastic deformation. Define 'spring-back' as the slight rebound that occurs as elastic strain releases. Introduce 'hem' and 'moment of inertia' as geometric strategies that dramatically increase structural stiffness without increasing material mass.
activities.studentsDo: In your workbook, match each of the 5 key engineering terms in the table to its correct definition from the definition bank provided.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each of the 5 terms in the table to its correct definition from the definition bank. Write the matching definition in the Match column.
activities.questioning: Why does a piece of sheet metal rebound slightly after releasing the bending force? Expected: The inner and outer fibres experience elastic strain that recovers once clamping pressure is removed, causing spring-back. How does folding a hem along a flat edge change its resistance to bending? Expected: It redistributes material away from the neutral axis, increasing the moment of inertia and cross-sectional stiffness.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Elastic Deformation: Temporary shape change where material returns to its original form once the load is removed.
- Plastic Deformation: Permanent structural change where the material retains the new shape after force exceeds the yield point.
- Spring-back: Residual elastic recovery that causes sheet metal to reopen slightly after bending force is released.
- Hem: A folded edge of sheet metal providing structural rigidity, safety, and a doubled-thickness border.
- Moment of Inertia: A geometric property of a cross-section indicating its resistance to bending and deflection under load.

activities.title: Pan Brake Setup and Pinch Points
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the workshop Pan Brake. Model mandatory PPE (safety glasses and leather handling gloves). Demonstrate the 4-step folding procedure: 1. Position sheet metal datum line against the clamping fingers; 2. Lock clamping lever with firm, even pressure; 3. Lift apron/swing leaf smoothly past 90 degrees to initiate the hem; 4. Flatten the hem by placing it beneath the clamping fingers and applying full downward clamping force. Emphasise danger zones: apron pinch points and finger crush hazards. Expected: The hem width will be inaccurate, resulting in an uneven safety edge that deviates from the drawing.

Pan Brake Operation Rules:
1. Alignment: Scribe line aligned exactly to edge of clamping fingers.
2. Clamping: Engage toggle clamp fully until it cams over into locked position.
3. Swing Leaf: Lift with both hands on handle bars; maintain controlled movement.
4. Hem Flattening: Re-position pre-bent lip under flat clamping fingers to squash flat.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how to measure a fold angle using an engineers' square and protractor against the light. Model the iterative decision path: 'If the angle is 87 degrees, the metal has sprung back and is under-bent. We re-insert the workpiece, align it, and pull the bending beam 2 degrees further. If it is 93 degrees, it is over-bent, which work-hardens the metal and is difficult to reverse.' Co-construct the fold audit workflow with the class.

activities.questioning: Why should you check the fold with an engineers' square before unclamping the workpiece completely? Expected: It allows rapid re-bending if under-bent without losing your original alignment against the clamp bar. Why is over-bending 0.6mm galvanised steel past 90 degrees considered a critical error? Expected: Bending it backwards to correct it work-hardens the fold line, which weakens the metal and can cause cracking or surface crazing of the zinc coating.

1. Measure fold against datum base with engineers' square.
2. Angle = 90 deg (+/- 1 deg): Proceed to next fold.
3. Angle < 90 deg (Under-bent): Re-clamp and apply incremental 1 to 2 deg over-bend.
4. Angle > 90 deg (Over-bent): Flag as non-conformance; lightly tap on wooden block under teacher guidance.

activities.title: Physics of Resistance Welding
activities.teacherDoes:
Explain Joule's Law of heating (Q = I^2 x R x t) using the board to demonstrate how current, resistance, and time govern heat generation. Emphasise that contact resistance between the two sheet metal faces generates localised heat above the steel melting point (approx 1450 degrees Celsius), while water-cooled copper electrodes remain cool and apply forging pressure to consolidate the joint.

Model Example:
Teacher: 'Notice how the electrode is copper. If it were steel, the electrode itself would melt. Because copper has ultra-low electrical resistance, the heat concentrates right at the boundary between our galvanised steel dustpan sheets where the resistance is highest.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the definition table by matching the five technical spot welding terms to their correct descriptions using the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the technical terms in column one. Select the matching description from the definition bank and write it in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why are spot welder electrode tips made of copper rather than steel?
expected: Copper has very low electrical resistance and high thermal conductivity, ensuring heat builds up in the high-resistance steel sheets rather than melting the electrode tips.
prompt: What is the specific role of mechanical pressure before, during, and after current flow?
expected: Pressure forces sheet surfaces into intimate electrical contact, contains the molten metal pool during the weld cycle, and forges the solidifying weld nugget to eliminate internal voids.
activities.scaffolding:
Full definitions for reference:
- Electrode: Water-cooled copper alloy conductor that concentrates electrical current and mechanical force onto the workpiece.
- Weld Nugget: The localised molten and resolidified steel core that forms the permanent structural joint between sheets.
- Contact Resistance: Electrical opposition at the overlapping sheet metal interface that converts electrical energy into thermal heat.
- Forging Pressure: Mechanical clamping force required to consolidate molten steel into a dense, void-free joint.
- Zinc Fume Extraction: Local exhaust ventilation required to capture hazardous vaporised zinc coating emissions during galvanised steel welding.

activities.questioning: Why will a drill bit wander or skate across sheet metal if no centre punch divot is used? activities.title: Isometric vs Perspective Conventions
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define isometric and perspective projection on the board. Illustrate how perspective lines converge toward a vanishing point, distorting true measurements, whereas isometric lines remain parallel along 30-degree axes to preserve 1:1 manufacturing scale. activities.questioning:
q: Why do engineers and sheet metal fabricators choose isometric projection over perspective drawings for technical specifications?
Expected: Isometric projection preserves true scale along all three primary axes, allowing direct measurement of dimensions.
q: What is the specific angular separation between the primary axes in an isometric projection?
Expected: The three axes are separated equally by 120 degrees, set at 30 degrees to the horizontal datum line.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Isometric Projection: An axonometric projection where three coordinate axes appear equally foreshortened at 120 degrees apart (30 degrees above the horizontal datum), preserving true measurement scale along all axes.
- Perspective Projection: A pictorial drawing method where receding parallel lines converge toward one or more vanishing points to simulate human optical depth, distorting dimensional scale.

activities.title: Defining Quality Management Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the core concepts of Quality Assurance (QA), Quality Control (QC), and Standard of Finish. Display the definitions on the board. Why is prioritising Quality Assurance more cost-effective for a commercial sheet metal manufacturer than relying solely on Quality Control? Expected: QA identifies tooling misalignment and process errors before materials are processed, preventing scrap metal and wasted labour, whereas QC only catches defective products after production costs have already been incurred.
How does a high standard of finish provide evidence of sound Quality Assurance throughout fabrication? Expected: A clean surface free of deep scribe scratches, heat tint, and ragged burrs demonstrates that correct machine calibration, careful clamping, and deburring protocols were followed at every manufacturing stage.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions provided on board:
- Quality Assurance (QA): Proactive, process-oriented activities designed to ensure manufacturing procedures prevent defects during production.
- Quality Control (QC): Reactive, product-oriented inspection procedures conducted on the completed prototype to verify dimensional compliance with specifications.
- Standard of Finish: The measurable aesthetic and tactile quality of a fabricated product's surfaces, safety hems, deburred edges, and welded joints.

activities.title: Commercial Quality Systems in Sheet Metal
activities.teacherDoes:
Present industrial quality systems used in sheet metal fabrication. Model how commercial workshops maintain calibration records for pan brakes, conduct destructive peel tests on spot welds prior to assembly runs, and enforce strict dimensional tolerances. Demonstrate how to extract key vocabulary to complete the cloze passage.

Example script:
'Notice how precision manufacturing depends on establishing exact parameters before production begins. For instance, if our sheet metal bender is out of alignment, every single dustpan fold will compound that error. Follow along with the guided notes to identify how quality assurance relies on systematic checks.'
activities.studentsDo: Track the guided presentation and fill in the missing terms in the cloze passage using the provided word bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze passage on industrial quality systems using the exact terms from the word bank.
activities.questioning:
If a pan brake stop is misaligned by 1.5 mm during the hemming operation, how does this QA failure affect subsequent assembly stages? Expected: The folded side flaps will not align squarely with the back panel, causing gap discrepancies and misaligned spot-weld tabs that fail QC inspection.
Why do sheet metal fabricators conduct test welds on scrap offcuts prior to joining finished workpieces? Expected: To verify that weld time, electrode pressure, and electrical current settings achieve full metal fusion without burning through the galvanised zinc layer.
activities.scaffolding:
Word Bank: tolerances, calibration, dimensional, preventive, standard.
Key definitions:
- Calibration = adjusting equipment against a known standard.
- Tolerances = permissible limit of dimensional variation (+/- 1.0 mm).
- Quality Assurance (QA) = proactive processes implemented to prevent defects before production.
- Quality Control (QC) = reactive inspection processes checking finished work against specifications.

activities.title: Standard of Finish Defect Critique
activities.teacherDoes: Display high-resolution photographs of three common sheet metal finishing defects on the projector: heavy scriber scratch marks across a flat face, weld spatter and heat discoloration around spot-welded tabs, and sharp wire burrs along a hemmed edge. Model a structured technical critique for Defect 1: identify the visible fault, explain the root cause, and specify the exact trade tool, abrasive grade, or chemical solvent needed to restore a commercial finish without stripping the zinc coating.

activities.visibleInstructions: In your workbook, identify each of the three projected manufacturing defects and specify the exact workshop tools, abrasives, or cleaning agents required to rectify them.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must fine-grade emery cloth (400-grit) or scotch-brite pads be used when removing layout marks rather than coarse abrasive paper?
Expected: Coarse abrasives cut through the thin protective zinc coating, exposing the raw ferrous steel beneath to atmospheric moisture and causing premature oxidation.
q: What functional risk does an unchamfered, burred edge pose on the finished dustpan?
Expected: Sharp wire burrs create a laceration hazard for the end user and prevent the dustpan lip from sitting flush against flat floor surfaces.

- Technical Remedies: Fine-grade emery cloth (400-grit) buffed along grain; isopropyl or citrus-based metal cleaner; draw-filing with smooth flat bastard file at 45 degrees; mallet dressing against a stake.

activities.title: Demonstrating Precision Dimensional Auditing
activities.teacherDoes:
Gather students at the central demonstration bench. Demonstrate how to inspect a fabricated dustpan against engineering drawings using digital vernier calipers, an engineers' square, and a steel rule. Model how to check the external caliper jaws for zero calibration, position the jaws square across the rear wall (nominal 200 mm), and read the dimension without parallax error. Demonstrate recording the nominal dimension (200 mm), measured dimension (200.8 mm), variance (+0.8 mm), and compliance status (Pass: within +/- 1.0 mm tolerance). Show how to annotate critical audit zones on the engineering diagram.

Script: 'Notice how my digital calipers are zeroed before touching the metal. When measuring the 200 mm rear base width, I ensure the jaw faces sit flat against the folded edges rather than the rounded corner radius. If the reading is 200.8 mm, our variance is +0.8 mm, which passes our +/- 1.0 mm tolerance band.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the caliper zeroing, jaw placement perpendicular to fold lines, and tolerance calculation methods. Annotate the four critical audit zones in the workbook diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration carefully. Use your workbook to annotate the four measurement zones on the engineering diagram, noting the inspection tool and critical tolerance check for each location.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must caliper jaws be placed perpendicular rather than skewed across the folded sheet metal flanges?
expected: Angling the jaws measures a diagonal hypotenuse rather than the true width, introducing an artificially high reading that misrepresents dimensional accuracy.
question: How does an engineers' square verify whether a fold angle meets manufacturing specifications?
expected: Placing the stock against the base and the blade against the upright wall reveals any light gaps, indicating an under-fold (<90 degrees) or over-fold (>90 degrees).
activities.scaffolding:
Calipers zeroing checklist:
1. Wipe jaw faces clean with a lint-free cloth to remove debris.
2. Close jaws gently and confirm digital readout displays 0.00 mm (press ZERO if required).
3. Keep workpiece stable on the workbench; avoid measuring hand-held components in mid-air to prevent flexion errors.

activities.teacherDoes: Lead a guided discussion to establish the definitive quality audit checklist. Prompt students to define clear pass/fail thresholds for dimensional tolerance (+/- 1.0 mm), joint integrity (rigid spot welds with zero mechanical play), safety standards (fully closed hems, deburred edges), and surface finish (complete removal of marker dye and scriber lines). Model how to verify a +/- 1.0 mm tolerance using digital calipers across the dustpan base width. Record accepted wording on the board while students populate their workbook checklists.

activities.visibleInstructions: Complete your quality audit checklist by verifying the four core criteria categories: Dimensional, Structural, Safety, and Aesthetic finish.
activities.questioning:
q: What specific criteria determine whether a spot-welded handle passes structural inspection?
Expected: The weld nuggets must show continuous metal fusion with zero relative movement when moderate manual torque is applied, and no burn-through holes in the steel sheet.
q: What defines an acceptable leading edge safety hem on the dustpan?
Expected: The 6 mm hem must be folded completely flat against the base sheet with no bowing, sharp burr protrusions, or open pockets that could trap debris.
activities.scaffolding:
Quality Criteria Framework:
- Dimensional: All folds and widths within +/- 1.0 mm of nominal drawing specifications.
- Structural: Handle spot welds fused securely; no peeling or joint deflection.
- Safety: Leading hem flattened; all cut edges deburred and corner radii chamfered.
- Aesthetic: No permanent marker lines, scriber gouges, or oxidation soot visible.

activities.teacherDoes:
Supervise workshop benches, enforcing eye protection and safe material handling. Circulate to verify students use calipers correctly without overtightening thumbwheels. Demonstrate light circular buffing using 400-grit emery cloth and approved metal cleaner to lift layout marker without scouring the zinc coating. Ensure students record actual measured values and compute variance in their workbook audit tables.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'When measuring the base width, place the fixed jaw firmly against the fold line and slide the vernier until it meets the opposite edge. If the nominal is 200 mm and your digital caliper reads 201.2 mm, your variance is +1.2 mm. Record this in your table and mark the tolerance column as No if our strict limit is +/- 1.0 mm.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct physical measurements on the fabricated dustpan, record nominal versus actual measurements in the table, verify tolerance compliance, and use emery cloth and metal cleaner to polish surfaces to a commercial standard.
activities.visibleInstructions: Measure your dustpan features using calipers and steel rules. Record nominal, measured, and variance data in your workbook table. Then use fine emery cloth and metal cleaner to remove all layout marks and weld soot.
activities.questioning:
prompt: If your measured base width is 201.8 mm against a nominal 200 mm drawing dimension, does it pass or fail our tolerance threshold?
Expected: It fails the tolerance threshold because the variance of +1.8 mm exceeds the permissible limit of +/- 1.0 mm; this variance must be recorded and evaluated in the folio.
prompt: Why must surface cleaning with emery paper follow the linear grain of the rolled sheet metal rather than circular swirls?
Expected: Linear polishing blends with the existing grain texture of the galvanised sheet, preventing visible swirl scratches and preserving an even aesthetic finish.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Calculation Formula:
Variance = Measured Dimension - Nominal Dimension.
If -1.0 mm <= Variance <= +1.0 mm -> Compliant (Pass).
If Variance > +1.0 mm or < -1.0 mm -> Non-compliant (Document in folio evaluation).

activities.title: Auditing AS 1100 Drafting Standards
activities.teacherDoes: Project a student drafting exemplar alongside an unrefined drawing containing common drafting errors (e.g. crossing dimension lines, inconsistent lowercase lettering, missing projection symbols). Demonstrate how to audit a drawing against AS 1100 conventions: line weight hierarchy (0.5 mm object outline vs 0.3 mm dimension line), 1.5 mm gaps between object edges and extension lines, Style A uppercase technical lettering, and title block completeness.

activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your Technical Drawing Booklet against the AS 1100 drafting checklist, ticking each verified convention and noting any corrections needed.
activities.questioning:
Why must extension lines never directly touch the physical outline of the component in an orthogonal drawing?
Expected: Leaving a 1.0–1.5 mm gap prevents extension lines from visually merging with the component boundary, ensuring drawing geometry remains distinctly readable.
What is the purpose of enforcing standardised Style A uppercase lettering on all drawing titles and dimensions?
Expected: Uppercase block lettering eliminates ambiguity between characters, preventing costly misinterpretations of critical dimensions during manufacturing.
activities.scaffolding:
Drafting Standards Reference:
- Object Lines: 0.5 mm / HB, solid, dark.
- Dimension & Projection Lines: 0.25–0.3 mm / 2H, sharp, thin, light.
- Lettering: 3 mm or 5 mm capital block lettering using 0.5 mm HB lead.
- Title Block: Name, Drawing Title, Scale (1:1 or 1:2), Date, Projection Symbol (3rd Angle).

orientate.smartStart: Complete the 3-minute silent retrieval challenge in your workbook: write the standard manufacturing tolerance used throughout this unit (+/- 1.0 mm) and list two functional consequences if a dustpan's contact edge is distorted.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can measure and evaluate the functional performance and dimensional accuracy of my completed dustpan against design criteria

activities.title: Modelled Evaluation & Quality Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how to conduct physical quality checks on a sample dustpan. Place the dustpan onto the precision steel surface plate. Demonstrate sliding a 0.5 mm feeler gauge under the contact lip to measure edge gap. Demonstrate checking the 90-degree fold angles using an engineer's square. Demonstrate verifying the spot weld join using a gentle manual deflection test (checking for joint separation or weld pop). Emphasise the assessment criteria targets: edge gap < 1.0 mm, fold angles 90° (+/- 1.5°), and spot welds completely secure with zero flex.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration of precision testing techniques on the surface plate and complete the testing standards reference table in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the three functional test demonstrations on the surface plate. In your workbook, fill in the blank measurement methods and standard targets for edge gap, fold angle, and spot weld integrity.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must the contact edge gap remain strictly below 1.0 mm across the entire front width?
expected: Any gap larger than 1.0 mm allows fine debris and dust to sweep underneath the pan instead of collecting inside.
q: What does an engineer's square reveal when placed against the side fold that a standard plastic ruler cannot?
expected: It reveals true perpendicularity (90 degrees) against a flat datum face and shows daylight if the fold angle has experienced spring-back.
activities.scaffolding: Evaluation criteria definitions: 1. Contact Edge Gap: maximum clearance between the sheet bottom lip and datum surface plate. 2. Fold Angle: angular deviation from 90 degrees measured on internal corners. 3. Spot Weld Integrity: mechanical retention of handle bracket under manual deflection load.
activities.eLearning: Display high-contrast visual testing setup on projector with callout arrows identifying feeler gauge placement.
activities.transition: Collect your steel rule, feeler gauge, and engineer's square from the tool rack and pair up with your bench partner.

activities.title: Guided Collaborative Testing
activities.teacherDoes:
Circulate among workshop benches while student pairs execute physical testing. Monitor correct tool handling: ensuring feeler gauges are inserted flat rather than forced at an angle, and engineer's squares are seated against the datum face. Prompt students to re-measure any ambiguous gaps and verify each other's recorded millimetre values before logging them.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'When measuring the contact edge gap, ensure the steel rule is flat against the workbench surface. If using a 0.5 mm feeler gauge, it should slide into the tolerance gap without forcing the folded sheet metal upward. Record your exact reading in the table.'
activities.studentsDo: Work in pairs to conduct physical measurements on both dustpans using steel rules, feeler gauges, and engineer's squares. Record the exact measured numbers and assign pass/fail status in the workbook audit table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Test both dustpans with your partner. Place the dustpan flat on the bench, test the contact edge with feeler gauges, check the side folds with the square, and check the handle spot welds. Record your exact numerical values and write Pass or Fail in the table.
activities.questioning:
question: If your feeler gauge measures a 2.0 mm gap on the left corner but 0.2 mm in the centre, what manufacturing operation caused this variation?
expected: Uneven clamping pressure on the pan brake during the hemming or folding operation, or distortion caused when cutting the sheet with hand shears.
question: Why must we record exact numerical measurements rather than just writing 'Pass' or 'Fail'?
expected: Numerical data provides empirical evidence required in design engineering to quantify tolerances and justify manufacturing evaluations.
activities.scaffolding: Measurement benchmarks: Feeler gauge blades: 0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm, 0.8 mm, 1.0 mm. Pass criteria: Gap <= 1.0 mm; Angle = 88.5°–91.5°; Handle offset <= 1.5 mm.
activities.eLearning: Ensure digital devices remain away from bench testing areas to maintain clear physical workspace.
activities.transition: Return workshop testing tools to shadow boards and open your workbook to the Independent Performance Summary section.

activities.title: Independent Performance Summary
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to write an evaluative justification connecting physical test results to manufacturing processes on the whiteboard. Provide the sentence frame: 'My contact edge recorded a gap of [X] mm because during the [operation], [specific cause] occurred.' Circulate the room from the rear to inspect student written justifications, prompting students who write superficial answers ('it worked fine') to cite specific measurements and tools.
activities.studentsDo: Work individually to write a two-section evaluative performance summary in the workbook, directly justifying their measured tolerances and detailing specific workshop modifications.
activities.visibleInstructions: Independently complete the two sections in your workbook. In Section 1, justify your physical measurement results using exact data from your audit table. In Section 2, specify an actionable workshop improvement strategy for future sheet metal fabrication.
activities.questioning: How did your initial marking-out scribing directly affect the angle of your pan-brake folds? Expected: If the scribed line had width or was angled slightly off the datum edge, the pan brake clamping fingers clamped off-parallel, creating a twisted bend. What corrective workshop strategy eliminates spring-back when folding 0.6 mm galvanised steel? Expected: Over-bending the sheet metal slightly past 90 degrees (to approximately 92 degrees) so it relaxes back to a true 90-degree corner.
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence starters for workbook sections:
- Section 1: 'My physical contact edge achieved a measured gap of ___ mm against the 1.0 mm target, which occurred because during the folding phase...'
- Section 2: 'To achieve tighter manufacturing tolerances in future sheet metal projects, I would modify my pan brake setup by...'
activities.eLearning: Timer projected on board. Laptops closed; solo written work in workbook.
activities.transition: Cap your pens and check that your dustpan is labelled with your student ID tag on the handle.

activities.title: Technical Photography Standards & Feedback Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the setup of a clean tabletop photography station using neutral backing card and diffuse workshop lighting. Model capturing three mandatory technical views on a sample dustpan: 1. Isometric Assembly (showing full 3D proportions and corner joints), 2. Spot Weld Detail (macro close-up showing nugget formation, spacing, and zero burn-through), and 3. Datum Contact Lip (front elevation against a white horizontal surface verifying edge contact). Explicitly demonstrate the constructive feedback protocol: 'Technical Achievement' (identifying accurate folds, neat deburring) and 'Area for Refinement' (identifying tolerance deviations, weld discoloration, or edge burrs).
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's photography setup and framing demonstrations, then complete the photographic standards audit table in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Watch the teacher demonstrate lighting, angles, and framing for the three required portfolio views. Complete the technical focus descriptions in your workbook audit table.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must folio photographs be captured against a neutral, uncluttered background rather than directly on a cluttered workshop bench?
expected: A neutral background removes visual distractions and allows assessors to clearly inspect edge straightness, fold lines, and weld quality.
prompt: Why is a macro close-up of the spot weld required in addition to an overall isometric shot?
expected: The overall shot cannot show joint penetration, heat marks, or nugget integrity, which are critical QCAA marking criteria for joining techniques.
activities.scaffolding:
Required photograph specifications:
- View 1: Isometric Assembly (45-degree angle, complete product in frame, showing depth and side folds).
- View 2: Macro Spot Weld Detail (within 100 mm, focused on weld indentations and bracket alignment).
- View 3: Datum Contact Lip (eye-level elevation against flat ground to demonstrate contact flatness).

activities.title: Peer Review Gallery Walk
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a structured peer review rotation. Assign each student to critique two peer dustpans at adjacent benches for 7 minutes each. Enforce the use of technical vocabulary: 'datum', 'burr-free', 'hem allowance', 'nugget penetration', and 'dimensional tolerance'. Circulate between benches to review student written notes, redirecting non-specific feedback ('looks cool') to objective engineering observations.
activities.studentsDo: Rotate to two assigned peer dustpans. Closely inspect fold lines, edge finishes, and weld joins. Record objective, criteria-referenced feedback in the structured workbook sections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rotate to your assigned peer stations. Inspect dustpan 1 for 7 minutes, then dustpan 2 for 7 minutes. Complete the 'Technical Achievement' and 'Area for Refinement' sections in your workbook using precise metalwork terminology.
activities.questioning:
question: What specific physical evidence indicates that an edge was correctly draw-filed and deburred?
expected: The metal edge shows a smooth, satin finish with a consistent 45-degree chamfer and has no jagged burrs or wire edges catching when touched safely.
question: How can you tell if spot welding electrodes were held in contact for too long during fabrication?
expected: Deep indentation into the sheet metal, surface discoloration/pitting, or molten zinc flash expelled around the weld nugget.
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence frames for peer feedback:
- Technical Achievement: 'The prototype demonstrates high precision in [fold alignment / hem tightness / spot weld consistency], evidenced by [specific observation].'
- Area for Refinement: 'The [contact edge / handle centring / corner chamfer] shows a variance of approximately [X mm / X degrees], which could be resolved by [specific technique].'

activities.title: Core Sustainability & Lifecycle Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the core vocabulary required for the summative written evaluation. Review the definitions of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), Sacrificial Protection, and Scrap Optimisation. Model writing the definition for Life Cycle Assessment on the whiteboard, breaking it down into extraction, manufacture, consumer use, and end-of-life recycling. Explain that the workbook match table requires matching each term to its precise industry-standard definition from the bank.
activities.studentsDo: Match the three key sustainability terms in the workbook table by writing the corresponding letter from the definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the definition bank in your workbook. Match each sustainability term in the left column with its correct definition by writing the correct letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
question: How does the galvanising process directly support product sustainability even though zinc extraction requires energy?
Expected: The zinc sacrificial coating prevents rust and oxidation, extending the operational lifespan of the steel dustpan by decades and avoiding premature replacement.
question: What role does scrap optimisation play in the initial marking-out phase of manufacturing?
Expected: Nesting the pattern tightly against the edges of the sheet minimises offcut waste and reduces the total quantity of raw sheet metal consumed.
activities.scaffolding:
Term definitions:
- Life Cycle Assessment (LCA): Systematic analysis of the environmental impact of a product across raw extraction, manufacturing, use, and disposal.
- Sacrificial Protection: Electrochemical protection where a zinc coating oxidises preferentially to shield underlying ferrous steel.
- Scrap Optimisation: Strategic layout and nesting of pattern templates on raw stock to maximise material yield and minimise waste.
activities.eLearning: Project the steel lifecycle diagram comparing primary blast furnace extraction with secondary scrap recycling.
activities.transition: Now use these technical concepts to complete your guided lifecycle and safety reflection notes.

activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the synthesis of material science, workshop safety, and environmental stewardship. Read through the cloze passage sentence-by-sentence. Discuss how galvanised steel exhibits high circularity because steel and zinc can be separated and recycled in electric arc furnaces. Discuss how workshop health and safety (WHS) protocols—such as wearing leather gloves and using bench shears safely—prevent stock ruination and eliminate wasted energy and materials. Model an example of explaining how material selection impacts lifecycle phases.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is secondary electric arc furnace steel production substantially more sustainable than primary blast furnace processing?
Expected: Electric arc furnaces use recycled scrap metal and require approximately 75% less energy than smelting virgin iron ore in a blast furnace.
question: How does strict adherence to WHS protocols prevent environmental waste in a fabrication workshop?
Expected: Following safe procedures prevents cutting mistakes, incorrect folds, and ruined material that would otherwise be discarded as industrial scrap.
